disclaimer: This is a first look, not a decision about eligibility. Each program makes its own decision. The links take you to the official sources, so you can check the details before you apply.

rules.name: VA Aid and Attendance
rules.summary: A monthly addition to the VA pension for wartime veterans and their surviving spouses who need help with everyday activities. Income and net worth limits apply.
rules.amounts_note: The Maximum Annual Pension Rates (MAPR) and the net worth limit come from va.gov and apply from 12/01/2025 to 11/30/2026. They change every year, so it's worth re-checking them.

conditions.check: Your parent is a veteran or the surviving spouse of a veteran.
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, your parent is not a veteran or a veteran's surviving spouse, and this program is for them.

conditions.check: Service requirements: at least 1 day during a wartime period and the required length of active duty (90 days if service began before 09/08/1980, usually 24 months after). Full conditions: va.gov/pension/eligibility.
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, the service did not include a wartime period, which this pension requires.

conditions.check: Your parent needs another person's help with everyday activities (bathing, eating, dressing), including help needed because of memory loss; or spends most of the day in bed; or is in a nursing home because of lost mental or physical abilities; or has severely limited eyesight. A doctor confirms this on VA Form 21-2680. va.gov lists the need for help, not a diagnosis, so a dementia diagnosis on its own does not count.
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, your parent does not need help with everyday activities, for memory or any other reason, and does not live in a nursing home, which this benefit is meant for.

conditions.check: Net worth (excluding the home, one car and most furnishings, minus debts, including the spouse's assets) is at or below the VA limit.
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, net worth is above the VA limit. If some of it is the home or a car, it may not count, so it's worth checking.

conditions.check: Annual income compared with the Maximum Annual Pension Rate (MAPR). If income is higher, va.gov explains which expenses (for example, medical) can reduce the income that counts. Rates differ for families with dependent children.

rules.result_description: Possibly a fit. If the conditions hold, your parent may be able to apply for a VA pension with Aid and Attendance. The VA makes the decision after reviewing the claim.
rules.unlikely_description: Unlikely to apply, based on what you told us. The reasons are below. If an answer was a guess, it's worth checking the details on va.gov.
documents: DD214 or another military discharge document
VA Form 21-2680 (completed by a doctor)
VA Form 21-0779 if your parent is in a nursing home
Income and asset records for your parent (and spouse)
For a surviving spouse: marriage certificate and the veteran's death certificate

rules.name: Medicaid long-term care
rules.summary: Medicaid is the main payer for long-term care in the US, both in nursing homes and at home. For people 65 and older, income is usually assessed with SSI rules, and assets count too. Limits and programs depend on the state.
rules.amounts_note: Income and asset limits are set by each state, so they aren't listed here. Your state's Medicaid agency can tell you the current ones.

conditions.check: Age 65 or older, or a disability or blindness (medicaid.gov: these groups are assessed with SSI income rules).

Need for care: the state assesses whether a nursing-home level of care or care at home is needed. Help needed because of memory loss counts as a need for care in that assessment. Needs review: medicaid.gov does not publish the functional criteria; each state sets its own.
Income at or below the state limit.
Assets at or below the state limit. Giving away or selling assets below value within 5 years before applying can lead to a denial, so it helps to ask before moving money.

rules.result_description: Possibly a fit. Your parent may be able to apply for Medicaid long-term care. The state makes the decision.
rules.unlikely_description: Unlikely to apply, based on what you told us. The reasons are below. The state makes the final decision.
documents: Proof of identity and citizenship or immigration status
Income records (Social Security, pensions)
Bank statements and asset records for the last 5 years
Medical records showing the need for care

rules.name: Dependent Care Credit (IRS)
rules.summary: A tax credit for someone who pays for the care of a parent who can't look after themselves, so that the caregiver can keep working. The parent must be a dependent (or would be, except for their income) and live with you for more than half of the year.

conditions.check: Your parent can't take care of their own hygiene or nutrition, or needs full-time attention. The IRS counts being physically or mentally incapable of self-care, so help needed because of memory loss counts too; a diagnosis alone does not.
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, your parent does not need help with self-care, for memory or any other reason, which this credit requires.

conditions.check: Your parent lived with you for more than half of the year.
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, your parent lived with you for half of the year or less, and this credit needs more than half.

conditions.check: You provide more than 50% of your parent's total support for the year (the support test, IRS Pub. 501).
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, you provide 50% or less of your parent's support, and this credit needs more than half.

conditions.check: The care expenses are what lets you (and your spouse, if filing jointly) work or look for work.
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, the care expenses aren't tied to your work or job search, which this credit requires.

always_check: Possibly a fit, but tax rules have exceptions. A tax professional can confirm it for your situation.
rules.result_description: Possibly a fit. You may be able to claim the Dependent Care Credit for your parent's care. A tax professional can confirm it.
rules.unlikely_description: Unlikely to apply, based on what you told us. The reasons are below.
documents: Receipts and invoices for care with the provider's name, address and TIN/SSN
Proof of what you spent supporting your parent (for the 50% support test)
Form 2441 with your tax return

rules.name: VA Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers
rules.summary: A VA program for family caregivers of a veteran with a disability rating of 70% or higher who needs ongoing personal care. The primary caregiver may receive a monthly stipend, training and support.
rules.amounts_note: The stipend depends on the level of care and the region. va.gov has the details.

conditions.check: Your parent is a veteran who was discharged from the military (or has a medical discharge date).
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, your parent is not a veteran, and this program is for veterans' caregivers.

conditions.check: VA disability rating (individual or combined) of 70% or higher.
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, the VA disability rating is below 70%, which this program requires.

conditions.check: The veteran needs personal care services, whether because of a physical condition or because of memory loss.
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, the veteran does not need personal care, for memory or any other reason, which this program is meant for.

conditions.check: The veteran needs at least 6 months of continuous, in-person personal care.
The veteran is enrolled in VA health care.
The caregiver is at least 18 years old and is a family member of the veteran (spouse, son, daughter, parent, step or extended family), or lives full time with the veteran or is willing to.

rules.result_description: Possibly a fit. Your family may be able to apply for the VA caregiver support program. The VA makes the decision.
rules.unlikely_description: Unlikely to apply, based on what you told us. The reasons are below.
documents: VA Form 10-10CG (a joint application, completed by the veteran and the caregiver together)
The veteran's military service records
Medical records showing the need for care

rules.name: Medicare Savings Programs and Extra Help
rules.summary: Medicare Savings Programs (QMB, SLMB, QI, QDWI) help pay Medicare premiums and costs. Extra Help pays part of Medicare Part D drug costs. Both are for people with income and resources below set limits.
rules.amounts_note: Limits are set federally or by the state. medicare.gov lists the current ones.

conditions.check: Your parent has Medicare (SLMB and QI need both Part A and Part B).
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, your parent does not have Medicare, and these programs are for people who do.

conditions.check: Income below the Medicare Savings Programs or Extra Help limit. Some states don't count part of the income, so it's worth applying even slightly above the limit.
Resources below the program limit.

always_check: Medicare Savings Programs are applied for through the state. Extra Help comes automatically with full Medicaid, state help paying Part B premiums, or SSI; otherwise you apply through Social Security. Details: https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/help/drug-costs
rules.result_description: Possibly a fit. Your parent may be able to get help paying Medicare costs or prescription drugs. The program makes the decision.
rules.unlikely_description: Unlikely to apply, based on what you told us: these programs are for people who have Medicare.
documents: Proof of income
Savings and bank statements
Medicare card

rules.name: Medicare before 65 (disability) and SSI
rules.summary: Two programs tied to a disability. Medicare: a person under 65 who receives Social Security disability benefits becomes entitled to Part A after 24 months of those benefits (right away with ALS). SSI: a monthly payment from Social Security for people who are 65 or older, blind, or disabled and have limited income and resources.
rules.amounts_note: SSI income and resource limits are set by Social Security and are not listed here: ssa.gov could not be checked automatically on 11/15/2026, so they stay blank until verified. ssa.gov/ssi has the current figures.

conditions.check: Your parent has a disability that limits work or daily activities, or is 65 or older (SSI also covers people 65+ without a disability).
conditions.fail_text: Based on your answers, your parent is under 65 and does not have a disability, and these programs are for people who are 65 or older, blind, or disabled.

conditions.check: Medicare before 65: entitlement to Part A begins after 24 months of Social Security disability benefits, or in the first month with ALS (cms.gov: Original Medicare eligibility; medicare.gov: when you can sign up). The 24 months count from when Social Security disability benefits begin, not from the diagnosis.
SSI: income below Social Security's limit. The limit is not listed here (needs review).
SSI: resources below Social Security's limit. The limit is not listed here (needs review).

always_check: Both programs run through Social Security. SSI eligibility details: https://www.ssa.gov/ssi. Medicare eligibility rules: https://www.cms.gov/medicare/eligibility-and-enrollment/origmedicarepartabeligenrol
rules.result_description: Possibly a fit. Depending on the disability decision and income, your parent may be able to get Medicare before 65 or SSI. Social Security makes both decisions.
rules.unlikely_description: Unlikely to apply, based on what you told us. The reasons are below.
documents: Social Security disability award letter, if there is one
Income records and bank statements
Medicare card, if your parent already has Medicare
